# R1. Sign-in and access

Everyone signs in; the signed-in person is who acts; the server enforces who may see and change what, with the rules Faro’s shared actions already enforce in code.

**Spec only.** Faro doesn’t build this: the internal app’s own platform provides the machinery, and this page says what it must do. It is part of the rebuild kit, not of Faro’s own requirements (`evals/requirements.json`).

## Why

Faro asks “Who are you?” once on each device and trusts the answer, and its public database key can still write to most tables (docs/mcp.md, “Until company sign-in arrives”). That is fine for a demo with made-up data and wrong for an app holding 15,000 people’s real goals: the change log must say who really did what, and a rule the browser checks can be skipped by anyone who calls the database directly.

The rules about who may do what already exist, once, in the shared actions the app and the AI assistant both call. The rebuild doesn’t need new rules; it needs them enforced where the records are stored, against a person the server knows.

## The rule

1. **Everyone signs in** (through the company’s sign-in, [R2](r2-single-sign-on.md)). There is no “Who are you?” and no “View as someone else”: the signed-in person is the actor for every action, and nobody chooses who they act as.
2. **Workspace membership is a person record.** A person belongs to a workspace when the workspace has a person record with their sign-in email (`Person.email`, lower case, one per workspace). Admins add people (Workspace or the People sheet); whoever creates a workspace is its first admin. Signing in with an email that matches no one: no workspace, and a message saying to ask an admin. Matching one: that workspace opens. Several: the person chooses. Marked as left (`leftAt`) or removed: no access to that workspace, and their AI tokens stop working.
3. **Reading is open inside a workspace.** Every member reads every goal, check-in, plan, ask, review, comment, person, team and the Activity log of their workspace, as in Faro today: nothing in Faro hides a goal from a member. The exceptions, as Faro has them: the list of AI tokens (an admin sees all, anyone else their own), Recently removed (an admin sees all, anyone else what they removed), the workspace’s feedback (admins), and the builder inbox (builders, rule 6; Faro opens its own on purpose). Someone who isn’t a member reads nothing of a workspace, not even that it exists.
4. **Changing follows the access table below**, which is what Faro’s shared actions enforce today. The server enforces it: a write the rules refuse is refused by the server (the database or the API), whatever sends it, with the same words the app shows. The browser’s own checks are only there to explain early. No key a browser holds can write.
5. **AI tokens are made on the server.** An admin makes one for a person; the secret is made by the server, shown once, and only its SHA-256 hash is kept. A token belongs to one person in one workspace and acts with exactly that person’s rights (the same access table); every change it makes is logged as that person, marked via MCP. The token’s person or an admin revokes it; it stops working when its person leaves. A token can’t create, switch or reset a workspace or choose who it acts as.
6. **Builder tokens and the builder inbox.** Builders are the people who look after the app itself (in the internal app, a group in the company directory). Only builders read the builder inbox: the markups and feedback people send about the app, from every workspace. A builder makes a builder token for themselves; it reaches the inbox as well as their workspace, and stops counting as one the moment they leave the builders. Someone who sent a markup or feedback sees its status (New, In hand, Fixed, Won’t fix), not other people’s. **Faro differs on purpose:** it never holds real data, so its inbox is open to anyone (Lane, 8 Nov, backlog O); the internal app must not copy that.
7. **Who may read a sent markup** (a markup about a goal sent to someone, backlog 3a). Its sender, the people it was sent to, and, when it was sent into a review, the people in that review. An admin of the workspace may remove one. Nobody else, watchers included. A markup is a picture of the sender’s screen, so it is only sent to people who can read everything on it: in the internal app, members of the same workspace. Its picture is kept private and read through a short-lived address the server makes for someone allowed to read it ([R4](r4-scale-and-safety.md), the master key).

## Who may change what

Read from Faro’s shared actions: each line names the function that enforces it today, in the app and the AI assistant alike. `src/spec/internal.test.ts` fails when an action that says who may do something isn’t listed here. Anything not listed, any member may do.

### Goals, plans and check-ins

| What | Who may | Enforced today by |
|---|---|---|
| Post or correct a check-in; change a goal or its plan (in a form, a spreadsheet, a bulk edit or through the AI) | The goal’s owner, or an admin | [`planChanges`](../../../src/domain/changeset.ts) |
| Add a goal | Anyone, for a goal they own; an admin, for anyone | [`planChanges`](../../../src/domain/changeset.ts) |
| Stop a goal that has check-ins (with a reason); delete one that has none | The goal’s owner, or an admin | [`stopGoal`](../../../src/domain/removal.ts), [`deleteGoal`](../../../src/domain/removal.ts) |
| Delete a goal’s latest check-in (after a newer one it can only be corrected) | Whoever posted it, or an admin | [`deleteCheckIn`](../../../src/domain/removal.ts), [`canDeleteCheckIn`](../../../src/domain/removal.ts) |
| Wrap up a goal at the end of the cycle | The goal’s owner, or an admin | [`saveRetro`](../../../src/domain/actions.ts) |
| Undo an import or bulk edit | Whoever made it, or an admin | [`undoImport`](../../../src/domain/removal.ts), [`canUndoImport`](../../../src/domain/removal.ts) |

### Comments and asks

| What | Who may | Enforced today by |
|---|---|---|
| Comment on a goal; agree an action on it | Anyone in the workspace | [`addNote`](../../../src/domain/actions.ts), [`addAction`](../../../src/domain/actions.ts) |
| Edit a comment | Whoever wrote it, only | [`editComment`](../../../src/domain/removal.ts) |
| Remove a comment | Whoever wrote it, or an admin | [`deleteComment`](../../../src/domain/removal.ts) |
| Ask a goal’s owner for an update, or a question | Anyone but the goal’s owner | [`askForUpdate`](../../../src/domain/actions.ts), [`askQuestion`](../../../src/domain/actions.ts) |
| Take back an ask for an update | Whoever asked, or an admin | [`undoUpdateAsk`](../../../src/domain/actions.ts) |
| Answer a decision or help, a question or an ask for an update | The person asked, or an admin; anyone, for an ask to no one in particular | [`answerRequest`](../../../src/domain/actions.ts), [`canAnswer`](../../../src/domain/asks.ts) |
| Mark an action done | Whoever does it, whoever asked for it, or an admin | [`markActionDone`](../../../src/domain/actions.ts), [`canMarkDone`](../../../src/domain/asks.ts) |
| Say a goal waits on another goal’s decision or help | The waiting goal’s owner, or an admin | [`linkRequest`](../../../src/domain/actions.ts) |
| Withdraw an ask | Whoever asked, or an admin; for a decision or help, also the owner of the goal it was raised on | [`withdrawRequest`](../../../src/domain/actions.ts), [`canWithdraw`](../../../src/domain/asks.ts) |

|---|---|---|

| Restore something removed, stopped or marked as left (within 30 days) | An admin, or whoever removed it | [`restoreRemoved`](../../../src/domain/removal.ts) |
| Make an AI token for someone | Admins | [`createToken`](../../../src/domain/actions.ts) |
| Revoke an AI token | An admin, or the token’s person | [`revokeToken`](../../../src/domain/actions.ts) |
| Send feedback about the app | Anyone | [`sendFeedback`](../../../src/domain/actions.ts) |

## What Faro does today

- The app asks “Who are you?” and remembers the answer on the device (Help, “Saying who you are”; `src/screens/Start.tsx`).
- Every rule in the access table is checked in `src/domain/actions.ts`, `src/domain/removal.ts`, `src/domain/asks.ts` and the change engine (`src/domain/changeset.ts`), by the app and the MCP server alike, before anything is saved. The database doesn’t check them.
- The public key can still write to most tables (not tokens; it can only add markups and feedback). Tokens are made in the database by `okr_token_create` and found by hash (`okr_token_find`, migration 0024).
- Every workspace in the shared database is listed to anyone who opens the app (`SupabaseStore.workspaces` in `src/adapters/supabase/goalsStore.ts`).
- Faro’s inbox is open on purpose (backlog O, migration 0031): anyone, with no sign-in, reads every markup and piece of feedback and their pictures (a public-read bucket nobody can list), and changes a status through the one status rule, recorded as the person using the app and undoable; any token reaches it through MCP. There is no builder sign-in and no builder token in the app any more (the builders list and builder tokens from migrations 0024 and 0029 are left in the database, unused). The internal app keeps rule 6 as written.
- Markups today are reports about the app; sending one about a goal (3a) is not built yet.

## Worked examples

An example marked **Faro today** is run against Faro’s code by `src/spec/internal.test.ts`: the result is what the code gives now. The others say what the internal app must do.

| Given | Then | Kind |
|---|---|---|
| Maya, not an admin, makes an AI token for herself. | refused: “Only admins can make tokens.” | **Faro today** |
| Maya, not an admin, changes Oskar’s job title. | refused: “Only admins can add people or change them.” | **Faro today** |
| Oskar, not an admin, renames the workspace. | refused: “Only admins can rename the workspace.” | **Faro today** |
| Oskar, not an admin, deletes the workspace, giving its name exactly. | refused: “Only admins can delete the workspace.” | **Faro today** |
| Oskar asked Maya for a decision. May Oskar, Maya and Priya (an admin) answer it? | Oskar no, Maya yes, Priya yes | **Faro today** |
| Priya asked Oskar to do an action. May Oskar, Priya and Maya mark it done? | Oskar yes, Priya yes, Maya no | **Faro today** |
| Oskar raised a decision on Maya’s goal, and also asked her for an update on it. May Maya withdraw each? | the decision yes, the update no | **Faro today** |
| Someone signs in as Maya.Patel@Example.com, and Maya’s person record has maya.patel@example.com. | They are Maya: emails are compared in lower case. | Required |
| Oskar is marked as left in Platform, and still has a token. | He can’t open Platform, and his token is refused at once. | Required |
| Maya sends a markup of her goal’s chart to Oskar. | Maya and Oskar can read it; Priya, an admin, can remove it but it isn’t in her list; someone watching the goal can’t see it. | Required |
| A script with the browser’s public key writes a check-in to Maya’s goal. | The server refuses it: the public key can’t write. | Required |

## Acceptance checks

1. For every line of the access table, someone outside its “who” is refused by the server, called directly with their own sign-in (not through the app), with the words the app shows. Someone inside it is allowed.
2. Every table refuses a write made with the public key, and every read of a workspace by someone who isn’t a member returns nothing.
3. Opening the app without signing in shows the sign-in, never a workspace or a list of workspaces.
4. A person marked as left can’t open the workspace, and a request with their token is refused within a minute of their leaving.
5. A token’s secret appears once, in the answer that made it, and nowhere stored: the database holds its SHA-256 hash.
6. Every change in the change log names the signed-in person (or the token’s person, marked via MCP); no change names someone else.
7. In the internal app: a builder token reads the builder inbox; an ordinary token, an admin’s included, is told it isn’t a builder token. Removing a builder from the builders stops their token reaching the inbox at once. (Faro’s open inbox fails this check on purpose.)
8. A sent markup is readable by its sender, its recipients and (sent into a review) the review’s people, and by nobody else; its picture’s address stops working after it expires.

## Nearest rebuild stage

[Stage 2: the core data and the change engine](../../rebuild/stage-2-core-data.md): access is enforced where the records are stored and changed. The rules themselves are the shared actions and the change engine; stage 3’s screens only explain them.

## Decided while writing it

- Reading stays open to every member of a workspace, as in Faro; private goals would be a new product rule, not in Faro.
- A sent markup is read by its sender, recipients and (in a review) the review’s people; not by watchers. Admins can remove one. This answers 3a’s open question on watchers for the internal app.
- Only admins make AI tokens, as Faro’s code says today; anyone revokes their own.
- Faro opens its inbox to anyone (Lane, 8 Nov): it holds no real data, and Lane needs to read markups on any device. The internal app keeps the inbox to builders (rule 6).
